item.title: Bangladesh seeks answers after Saudi Arabia executes two of its citizens without notice
item.description:
Bangladesh seeks answers after Saudi Arabia executes two of its citizens without notice

Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Mon, 10/19/2026 - 12:59
Dhaka said it was not informed by Saudi Arabia that it had executed the pair arrested in Mecca for 'indecent acts'
Bangladeshi workers sitting outside an airport after flights to Saudi Arabia were cancelled following a series of Houthi attacks in October (AFP/Piyas Biswas)
Off

Bangladesh is seeking answers on why Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca without telling Dhaka.

Last week, Saudi Arabia executed a male and a female Bangladeshi national after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” inside a mosque.

Riyadh did not provide further details on the acts the two Bangladeshi nationals allegedly committed or whether they had legal representation in the Gulf kingdom, according to local media reports.

Reacting to the incident, Bangladesh’s minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters that he was “very disappointed” by the lack of communication and that Dhaka was seeking an explanation on why they were executed and not informed beforehand about the execution.

“We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday.

Earlier, the Bangladeshi foreign ministry said that it was waiting for a copy of the full verdict and the circumstances that led to the execution.

The official added that the two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh but did not indicate that they had planned to execute them.

Last week, Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court overturned the death sentence of a Sri Lankan national after he allegedly insulted Islam and the Prophet Muhammad.

Sri Lanka’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra confirmed that Riyadh had overturned the death sentence of Anojan Sivarasa.

The 27-year-old remains imprisoned after he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi Riyals ($800,000).

The court handed down the sentence amid intense criticism of Riyadh's legal system.

Saudi Arabia relies on interpretations of Islamic law, alongside cybercrime and counterterror legislation, to target online expression under the guise of protecting "public morals".

This has resulted in a surge of decades-long prison terms for social media users and an increased use of capital punishment.

At least 175 people have been executed so far this year, the majority of whom are foreign nationals.

item.title: Imran moves High Court, gets show-cause notice after ‘leave India’ order
item.description:
Bollywood Actor Imran Khan has approached the Bombay High Court after receiving an order from the Indian government directing him to leave the country.

Filing a petition before the High Court on Saturday (17 October), his lawyers argued that the order is arbitrary, unjustified and based on misconceptions. They stated that Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholders are not bound by any condition that bars them from staging protests.

The petition is likely to be heard on Monday (19 October) before a bench headed by Bombay High Court Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi. Imran has requested an expedited hearing.

The Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had ordered Imran to leave India by 28 October. Imran’s lawyers have described the order as ‘unconstitutional’.

Imran is accused of participating in a protest march organised by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) despite being a foreign national. The authorities reportedly issued the departure order on this ground.

He was informed that he is a US citizen and an OCI cardholder. Recipients of that status are not allowed to join anti-government protests in India.

Imran has challenged the order in the high court on several grounds. First, he argued that no such restriction applies to OCI cardholders. Second, he is not a member of any political party. Simply walking into a protest or speaking about the right to move freely cannot be treated as a crime. Third, he was ordered to leave the country without even being given a chance to explain his side.

He stated that the entire decision is unconstitutional, one-sided, and based on misunderstandings. The petition described the move as "the ultimate example of government arrogance and abuse of power."

Imran has urged the court to ensure that no coercive action is taken against him, that he is not forcibly deported and that no Look Out Circular (LOC) is issued against him pending the disposal of his petition.

Notably, on the same day Imran approached the Bombay High Court, the FRRO issued him another notice. The second notice is a show-cause letter asking why his OCI card should not be cancelled.

Imran’s lawyers see this as a significant point in their challenge. Questions have been raised as to why a show-cause notice was issued after he had already been ordered to leave the country.

The lawyers argue that the sequence raises questions about whether the initial order was issued without hearing his side. The second notice also suggests that the FRRO may not have followed the proper procedure and is now attempting to correct the error.

Imran’s lawyer, Zulfiqar Memon, told the media that they were reviewing the second notice. “The implications of the new notice will become clear during the court hearing. We will ask which notice should be considered valid, the first or the second. If the second notice is the relevant one, the first becomes ineffective,” he said.

In his petition, Imran has alleged that he is being made a scapegoat and suggested that there may be other reasons behind the action.

The petition invokes Article 14 of the Indian Constitution, which guarantees equality before the law, and Article 21, which protects the right to life and personal liberty. Seeking a stay on the notice, it argues that allowing the order to stand would violate the principles of natural justice and amount to a mockery of the Constitution.

The petition further alleges that the departure order was issued without adequate consideration and was based on an arbitrary decision.

Indian authorities can cancel an OCI card if they consider the holder’s activities to be prejudicial to the country’s sovereignty and security. Section 7D(e) of India’s Citizenship Act provides for such cancellation.

Imran Khan, 44, is an American citizen of Indian origin. He was born in Wisconsin, United States and is the nephew of popular Bollywood actor Aamir Khan.

item.title: Safeguarding national interests, sovereignty to remain Bangladesh's core commitment: PM
item.description:
Safeguarding national interests, sovereignty and dignity would remain the foremost commitment of Bangladesh in the days ahead, while the country seeks to strengthen friendship and cooperation with all nations on the basis of mutual respect and equality, said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday (18 October).

"Bangladesh wants to strengthen friendship and cooperation with all countries on the basis of mutual respect and equality," he said while addressing a National Standard Awarding Ceremony at Savar Cantonment this morning, where several battalions and regiments received the National Standard in recognition of their professional excellence.

Emphasising the significance of the award, the prime minister said the National Standard is not merely a flag, but a symbol of a unit's history, heritage, discipline, sacrifice, professionalism and commitment to the country.

"The glorious hoisting of the national flag constantly reminds us of our independence, sovereignty and the sacrifices of countless people," he said, adding that receiving the standard represents a renewed pledge to discharge assigned responsibilities with greater dedication.

"Safeguarding the honour of the flag is a sacred duty of every soldier," he said.

Turning to the requirements of a modern military, Tarique Rahman said its strength could not be measured merely by weapons, equipment or manpower.

"The true strength of a modern armed force lies in discipline, competence, leadership, integrity, training and public trust and, above all, in the chain of command," he said.

He said the government is continuing its efforts to build the armed forces into a more technology-driven, competent, disciplined, professional and modern force.

The prime minister also said the public expects officers and soldiers at all levels to remain steadfast in upholding the Constitution, laws, military regulations and humanitarian values while discharging their duties.

Highlighting the changing global security environment, he said the nature and strategies of warfare are evolving rapidly.

Alongside land, sea and air capabilities, cyberspace, outer space, drones, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare and information-based capabilities have become important components of national security.

"In this reality, work is underway to advance our defence preparedness in keeping with the changing times," he said.

The prime minister said the government attached importance to establishing a domestic defence industry to manufacture essential weapons, ammunition and defence equipment locally alongside modernising the army in all areas.

However, technology could never replace people, he said, adding, "We need to develop an integrated defence capability that would enable the army, navy and air force to operate in coordination when necessary, alongside enhanced technological capabilities."

Referring to the country's Liberation War, the prime minister said the history of the Bangladesh Army was inseparably linked with the birth of Bangladesh through the War of Liberation.

He recalled that on the night of 25 March 1971, when Pakistani forces launched a brutal crackdown on the freedom-loving people of Bangladesh, Major Ziaur Rahman, then deputy commander of the Eighth East Bengal Regiment in Chattogram, declared, "We revolt."

Tarique Rahman said Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman subsequently assembled Bengali-speaking officers and soldiers of the regiment and instructed them to join the armed struggle for independence.

Quoting Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman's article "The Birth of a Nation", the prime minister said Ziaur Rahman had written that he called the battalion's officers, junior commissioned officers (JCOs) and soldiers together and instructed them to take part in the armed struggle at 2:15 am on 26 March 1971.

The prime minister said Bengali-speaking members of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 8th East Bengal regiments had mounted armed resistance against the Pakistani occupation forces following the crackdown on 25 March.

He also recalled Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman's subsequent declaration of independence from Kalurghat Radio Centre on 27 March, saying his role in the War of Liberation remained an inspiring chapter for the armed forces.

Such a historic and courageous role by an army officer in the country's independence and Liberation War remained a source of pride and inspiration for the armed forces, he said.

"That is why patriotic people who cherish independence consider any success of the army a success for Bangladesh," he added.

The armed forces not only defend the country but also play important roles during natural disasters, fires and other national emergencies, he said. They were also serving with distinction in international peacekeeping missions.

The prime minister said the government is giving due importance to the welfare, housing, healthcare, education, training, career development and post-retirement social security of armed forces personnel.

He said salaries and allowances of armed forces members have already been increased by between 100 and 138 per cent under the national pay scale.

The implementation of the "One Rank, One Pension" system is also being processed to further improve the living standards of army personnel, he added.

Cabinet members and advisers, the army chief, representatives of the diplomatic corps, former and serving armed forces officers, and military personnel of different ranks attended the ceremony organised by the 9th Infantry Division.

item.title: Bridge Authority flags 14 factors behind Karnaphuli Tunnel’s losses
item.description:
A feasibility study for the Karnaphuli Tunnel project in Chattogram projected that an average of 28,305 vehicles would use the tunnel every day in 2025. However, only 4.172 million vehicles have used it in total since it opened. This translates to an average of just 3,865 vehicles crossing the tunnel each day.

The figures are presented in a report by the Bangladesh Bridge Authority. At the current level of traffic, toll revenue is insufficient even to cover the tunnel’s daily operating expenses. Operations and maintenance now cost an average of Tk 2.3 million a day, while daily revenue averages Tk 1.1 million.

The report identifies 14 reasons for the tunnel’s financial losses and outlines several measures to increase toll revenue.

Titled ‘Feasibility Study, Implementation and Current Financial Status of the Karnaphuli Tunnel,’ the report was submitted to the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Planning on Saturday. The committee has decided to examine the implementation of projects related to the tunnel and investigate the causes of its financial losses.

The Karnaphuli Tunnel was built at a cost of Tk 100 billion during the Awami League government. Vehicle movement through the tunnel began on 29 October 2023.

According to sources concerned, the report submitted to the parliamentary committee identifies the main reasons for the losses. These include inadequate road connectivity, limited capacity and insufficient development of connecting roads, failure to build the proposed deep-sea port at Sonadia in Cox’s Bazar, lack of a connection through the Marine Drive, failure to achieve planned urban development on the southern bank of the Karnaphuli River, industrialisation in Anwara falling short of expectations, and delays in implementing investments.

As a result, the expected volume of traffic has not materialised.
The report also cites several other factors: tourism facilities in Anwara have not developed as expected; the service area is not being used to its anticipated capacity; connections with the port and industrial zones remain inadequate; restrictions have been imposed on the movement of heavy-load vehicles; and drivers are apprehensive about the scanning process.
The report says several measures are being taken to increase the tunnel’s revenue. These include leasing out the service area, reducing operating costs and directing long-distance vehicles to use the Karnaphuli Tunnel instead of entering Chattogram city.

Construction is underway on seven jetties by Karnaphuli Dry Dock Limited as part of efforts to expand the operations of Chattogram Port. Three of the jetties are already operational. Once all seven are in service, they are expected to handle 10–12 million tonnes of cargo annually. This could increase the tunnel’s annual toll revenue by Tk 2–2.4 billion.

Construction of the China Economic and Industrial Zone was inaugurated on 27 July. Its first factory is expected to begin production within 18 months. This, too, is expected to increase vehicle traffic through the tunnel.

The committee meeting discussed the Karnaphuli Tunnel’s feasibility study, implementation and the reasons behind its current financial losses. The matter will be discussed in greater detail at the committee’s next meeting. It was decided that the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Planning would work towards a proper investigation into the implementation of tunnel-related projects and the causes of the current financial losses.

ADP implementation: 26 ministries and divs lag behind

At the meeting, a report by the Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division (IMED) of the Ministry of Planning showed that the national average rate of implementation of the Annual Development Programme (ADP) in the last fiscal year was 67.52 per cent.

Of the 56 ministries and divisions, 26 recorded implementation rates below the national average, while the remaining 30 performed above it.
The ministries and divisions that fell behind were Public Administration; Liberation War Affairs; Land; Cultural Affairs; Information; Primary and Mass Education; Youth and Sports; Environment; Religious Affairs; and Women and Children Affairs.

The list also included the Information and Communication Technology Division, Election Commission Secretariat, Economic Relations Division, Parliament Secretariat, Anti-Corruption Commission, Internal Resources Division, Health Services Division, Health Education and Family Welfare Division, Secondary and Higher Education Division, Technical and Madrasah Education Division, Prime Minister’s Office, IMED and Planning Division.

A list of projects whose completion deadlines were extended in the last fiscal year was also presented at the meeting. Members were informed that, at the previous meeting on 8 September, the committee had been told that extensions had been recommended for 256 projects in fiscal year 2025–26. The number subsequently rose to 288.


According to a press release from the Parliament Secretariat, the meeting discussed the reasons for extending the deadlines of 256 projects in fiscal year 2025–26. These included complications in land acquisition, dependence on imports, difficulties in appointing project directors, inadequate feasibility studies in many cases, delays in releasing funds for some projects, and conflicts between ministries.

The committee recommended that the relevant authorities take effective steps to address delays in implementing these projects.

Sources concerned said the Ministry of Planning informed the committee that a draft of a new policy on appointing project directors for government projects had been prepared. Once the policy takes effect, former officials and experts with relevant experience could be appointed as project directors.

The Parliament Secretariat’s press release said the ministry had informed the committee that work on the new policy was underway. It expressed hope that finalising the policy would help resolve persistent difficulties in appointing project directors.

Committee chairman Zahir Uddin Swapan chaired the meeting. Committee members, including State Minister for Planning Zonayed Saki, Kazi Rafiqul Islam, Moinul Islam Khan, Md Saiful Alam and Rashedul Islam, attended.

item.title: Chamber court stays order to recover Tk 6.66b in outstanding taxes from Grameen Kalyan
item.description:
Following a reassessment, the Appellate Division’s Chamber Court has stayed a High Court order to take steps to recover outstanding taxes from Grameen Kalyan for five tax years.

Chamber Judge of the Appellate Division Justice Md Rezaul Haque passed the order on Sunday in response to two separate leave-to-appeal petitions filed by Grameen Kalyan challenging separate High Court judgments.

According to the state, the outstanding tax demand against Grameen Kalyan for the five tax years amounts to Tk 6.66 billion.

The Chamber Court has also fixed 13 December for hearings on the two separate leave-to-appeal petitions filed by Grameen Kalyan against the High Court judgments. The hearings will take place before the regular bench of the Appellate Division.

Grameen Kalyan was founded by Professor Muhammad Yunus, the former chief adviser to the caretaker government, who also served as the organisation’s chairman.

On 10 September, the High Court dismissed two separate writ petitions filed by Grameen Kalyan, discharging the rules issued in connection with the legality of the tax commissioner’s decisions on the tax demands for the tax years 2012–13, 2013–14, 2014–15, 2015–16 and 2016–17 following reassessment.

The High Court bench comprising Justice Md Mojibur Rahman Miah and Justice Rezaul Karim delivered the judgments.

The full texts of the High Court judgments dismissing the two writ petitions filed by Grameen Kalyan were published on 12 October. One judgment runs to 15 pages, while the other is 32 pages long.

The concluding portion of the 32-page judgment directed the respondents, including the relevant tax commissioner in Dhaka, to take the necessary steps to recover the outstanding taxes from the petitioner, Grameen Kalyan, as soon as possible in accordance with the law.

The concluding portion of the 15-page judgment directed the respondents, including the relevant tax commissioner in Dhaka, to take the necessary steps regarding the outstanding tax by issuing a notice to the petitioner.

Following publication of the full judgments, Grameen Kalyan filed two separate leave-to-appeal petitions. Both petitions appeared on Sunday’s cause list of the Chamber Court.

Senior lawyers Fida M Kamal, Abdullah Al Mamun and Sardar Jinnat Ali represented Grameen Kalyan in court. Deputy Attorney General Mohammad Mehdi Hasan appeared for the state.

Following the court order, senior lawyer Abdullah Al Mamun told Prothom Alo that the Chamber Court had stayed the High Court’s directive to take the necessary steps to recover the outstanding taxes from Grameen Kalyan as soon as possible.

No steps can be taken to recover the money for the time being, he said.

The matter has been listed for hearing before the regular bench of the Appellate Division on 13 December. A final decision on the issue will follow the disposal of the leave-to-appeal petitions, he added.

Deputy Attorney General Mohammad Mehdi Hasan said the operative portions of the High Court’s directions in the two separate judgments had been stayed.

He told Prothom Alo that one judgment had directed the respondents to take the necessary steps to recover the outstanding taxes from the petitioner, Grameen Kalyan, as soon as possible. The other had directed them to take the necessary steps by issuing a notice concerning the petitioner’s outstanding tax liability.

The operative portions of both judgments have been stayed, he said, adding that the two leave-to-appeal petitions had been scheduled for hearing before the regular bench of the Appellate Division on 13 December.

Background to the case

According to lawyers familiar with the case, Grameen Kalyan entered into an agreement with Grameen Telecom under which investments were made in Grameenphone. Under the agreement, Grameen Kalyan was entitled to 42.65 per cent of the profits earned from dividends received on the shares.

However, questions arose over whether the money received constituted dividend income or income from other sources. The tax authorities maintained that the money was, in effect, interest or income earned from investments and should therefore be classified as “income from other sources”, rather than dividend income.

In 2017, Grameen Kalyan filed two separate writ petitions challenging the legality of the tax commissioner’s decisions concerning the tax demands for the five tax years following reassessment. After preliminary hearings, the High Court issued rules in the cases.

Following final hearings, the High Court disposed of the rules on 17 October 2023, issuing a judgment containing directions and observations.

The judgment set aside the tax commissioner’s orders. It also allowed Grameen Kalyan, subject to conditions and after condoning the delay, to file appeals within 60 days in accordance with the law before the appellate authority against the decisions of the additional tax commissioner.

The National Board of Revenue (NBR) subsequently filed separate leave-to-appeal petitions challenging the High Court judgment.

On 11 March 2024, the Appellate Division issued an order disposing of the separate leave-to-appeal petitions filed by the NBR. It directed the High Court to rehear the substantive issues raised in Grameen Kalyan’s writ petitions.

Following the rehearing, a High Court division bench delivered a judgment on 4 August 2024 dismissing the two writ petitions. However, the same bench recalled the judgment on 29 August that year.

The reason given was that the second judge on the division bench had previously contested the cases on behalf of the government while serving as a deputy attorney general. As he had represented one of the parties in the proceedings, the judgment was considered defective. The case records were subsequently sent to the Chief Justice.

In an order dated 13 May, the Chief Justice referred the matter to a division bench led by Justice Md Mojibur Rahman Miah for disposal.

After hearing the cases, the bench discharged the rules and delivered judgments containing directions. Following the separate leave-to-appeal petitions filed by Grameen Kalyan against those judgments, the operative portions of the High Court’s directions have now been stayed.

item.title: New secretariat to be built with 14 buildings in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar
item.description:
The Cabinet has given in-principle approval to a proposal to relocate the Bangladesh Secretariat to Sher-e-Bangla Nagar in the capital, where 14 12-storey buildings are planned on a 31.58-acre site currently occupied by the former trade fair ground.
The proposed complex will provide around 3.316 million square feet of office space and include three basement levels, parking for 3,800 vehicles, a mosque, multipurpose halls, a cafeteria and a post office. Around 30% of the project area is planned to be reserved for greenery and water bodies.
The Cabinet also approved the draft of a special ordinance on solar power installation, targeting 3,000-4,000 megawatts of rooftop solar capacity before next summer. At the same meeting, it approved a proposal to rename the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs as the Ministry of Women and Children, as well as Bangladesh’s proposed accession to the Rotterdam Convention on the international trade of hazardous chemicals and pesticides.
The decisions were taken at the Cabinet’s 25th meeting, chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Secretariat on Sunday. Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Gani briefed reporters on the decisions after the meeting.
The government had earlier taken an in-principle decision to relocate the Secretariat at a recent meeting chaired by the prime minister.
According to a Cabinet press release, the existing Secretariat has around 1.876 million square feet of office space. More than one million additional square feet are needed to meet the growing requirements of different ministries and accommodate ministries and divisions currently operating outside the Secretariat compound.
To address the shortage, the government has planned a new Secretariat in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar. Following a decision by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC), the Department of Architecture prepared a conceptual design for the complex at the former trade fair ground, in line with the master plan developed by Louis I Kahn.
Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Gani said the proposed complex would comprise 14 12-storey buildings on around 31.58 acres of land. The buildings, including three basement levels, would provide a total of approximately 3.316 million square feet of space.
The design includes parking for 3,800 vehicles, with 200 spaces above ground. The complex will also have a mosque, two multipurpose halls, each with a capacity of 350 people, a cafeteria and a post office.
Gani said around 30% of the project area would be allocated to greenery and water bodies.
The extent to which the new complex will ease the existing space shortage will depend on plans for relocating different ministries and divisions and the effective use of the new buildings.
The Cabinet has given in-principle and final approval to the draft Special Solar Power Installation Ordinance, 2026, aimed at reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels, easing the burden of subsidies and strengthening energy security.
The final approval is subject to vetting by the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division.
Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Gani said the government had set a target of installing 3,000-4,000 megawatts of rooftop solar capacity before next summer. To achieve this, instructions have been issued to install solar power systems on the rooftops of buildings owned by government, semi-government and autonomous bodies, local government institutions and state-owned companies.
The proposed framework provides for two financing models: Operational Expenditure (OPEX) and Capital Expenditure (CAPEX).
Under the OPEX model, an investor will install a solar power system using its own funds. Under the CAPEX model, institutions with their own revenue sources will be able to install solar systems based on projected future earnings.
According to the Cabinet press release, existing regulations do not provide sufficiently clear provisions on long-term electricity pricing, the use of electricity as payment for rooftop space, or maintenance arrangements when solar systems are installed by service providers under the OPEX model.
Similarly, existing laws lack clear provisions governing the installation of solar systems and the receipt of services under the CAPEX model.
The government has therefore initiated the new ordinance to establish rules governing investment, service delivery and maintenance in the sector. The proposed framework is expected to clarify investment arrangements and define the responsibilities of the parties involved in rooftop solar projects.
The Cabinet approved a proposal submitted by the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs to rename it the Ministry of Women and Children.
The Cabinet also approved a proposal submitted by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for Bangladesh to join the Rotterdam Convention, an international treaty governing trade in certain hazardous chemicals and pesticides.
The treaty, formally known as the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade, was adopted on September 10, 1998, and entered into force on February 24, 2004, according to the Cabinet press release.
The Cabinet briefing materials state that 167 countries have joined the convention. Among member states of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), all countries except Bangladesh and Bhutan are parties to the treaty.
Joining the convention is expected to strengthen Bangladesh’s capacity to manage hazardous chemicals, facilitate access to foreign funding for relevant projects, support the development of a chemical information database and improve the monitoring of chemical substances.
Membership would allow Bangladesh to make prior informed consent-based decisions on the import and export of chemicals listed in Annex III of the convention. It would also strengthen the framework for sharing responsibilities between importing and exporting countries in international trade.
Under Article 14, which deals with information exchange, Bangladesh would be able to exchange scientific, technical, economic and legal information on hazardous chemicals and pesticides with other member states.
Article 16 would also provide opportunities for Bangladesh to receive technical assistance from the Rotterdam Convention Secretariat to improve chemical management.
The Cabinet’s approval clears the way for Bangladesh to take the next steps towards joining the international treaty.

item.title: Cabinet approves relocation of Secretariat to Sher-e-Bangla Nagar by 2029
item.description:
The Cabinet has given in-principle approval to relocate the Bangladesh Secretariat to the former trade fair ground in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka, with government offices expected to begin operating at the new site in 2029.
The approval was given at a Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday.
According to the Cabinet Division, the new Secretariat complex will be built on 31.58 acres of land, featuring fourteen 12-storey buildings with three basement levels each. The complex will provide around 33.16 lakh square feet of office space.
The project will include parking facilities for 3,800 vehicles, with 200 spaces above ground and the rest underground. Other facilities will include a mosque, two multipurpose halls with a capacity of 350 people each, a cafeteria and a post office. Around 30% of the site will be reserved for greenery and water bodies.
The existing Secretariat occupies 17.57 acres and comprises 13 buildings, eight of which were built before independence, the Cabinet Division said. Buildings 1, 2, 3 and 8 were constructed between 1937 and 1939, while Building 5 was built in 1947.
The buildings were not designed to withstand earthquakes. As Dhaka lies in an earthquake-prone zone, housing key government ministries and divisions in these structures poses a safety risk, according to the Cabinet Division.
The existing complex also lacks adequate office space and toilet facilities for officials and employees. The number of users exceeds the buildings' capacity, making it difficult to maintain a healthy working environment.
The current Secretariat has around 18. 76 lakh square feet of office space. However, more than one million additional square feet is needed to meet the growing demands of ministries and accommodate those operating outside the complex.
The Cabinet Division said the initiative to build the new Secretariat at the former trade fair ground was taken following a decision by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec), in line with the master plan prepared by architect Louis I Kahn.
The Department of Architecture has already prepared a conceptual design for the proposed complex.
The Cabinet's in-principle approval clears the way for the proposed construction and relocation.

item.title: OIC backs Rohingya case, hopes for lasting solution
item.description:
Member states of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) have reaffirmed their support for the Rohingya genocide case before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), expressing hope that the legal proceedings will help pave the way for a lasting solution to the protracted crisis.
The renewed commitment came at a meeting of the OIC Ministerial Ad-Hoc Committee on Accountability for Human Rights Violations Against the Rohingya, held on the sidelines of the 52nd OIC Council of Foreign Ministers (CFM) in Baghdad, Iraq.
Addressing the meeting as co-chair, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir urged OIC member states to demonstrate greater unity and take proactive measures to resolve the longstanding Rohingya crisis.
Kobir, who is leading the Bangladesh delegation to the ministerial conference, stressed that ensuring justice and accountability through international legal mechanisms was essential to finding a sustainable solution to the humanitarian crisis.
Describing the Rohingya crisis as one of the major challenges confronting the Muslim Ummah, he called for a coordinated and collective response from OIC member states to strengthen humanitarian assistance and support ongoing legal efforts.
The state minister underscored the importance of sustained international engagement to ensure that the plight of the Rohingyas remains a priority on the global agenda.
He also drew attention to the five-point action plan presented by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
Referring to the action plan, Kobir emphasized the need for urgent and decisive international action, particularly to ensure justice and accountability through established legal frameworks.
He called upon OIC member states to translate their solidarity with the Rohingyas into concrete initiatives aimed at addressing the crisis and supporting efforts towards a durable solution.
At the meeting, OIC member states reiterated their commitment to supporting the case before the ICJ and expressed optimism that the judicial process would contribute to resolving the longstanding crisis.
The meeting highlighted the importance of collective international efforts to pursue accountability for human rights violations against the Rohingya and advance prospects for a lasting resolution.
Bangladesh has been hosting 1.4 million Rohingyas who fled persecution in Myanmar, while continuing diplomatic efforts to secure a sustainable solution to the crisis.

item.title: Kremlin says Ukrainian attacks won’t change war aims as Kyiv hits Saint Petersburg
item.description:
The Kremlin on Sunday said Ukrainian large-scale attacks on Russian cities will not change its war aims as Kyiv hit Saint Petersburg with the biggest drone attack on Vladimir Putin’s hometown since 2022, setting an oil refinery ablaze.
Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg’s historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot in night-time strikes that killed one person.
The attack came as Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of violating an “energy ceasefire” announced by US leader Donald Trump 76 times as he warned Russia planned a “blackout” in Ukraine before winter.
Kyiv struck Saint Petersburg as its ties with Washington strained massively in recent days, with Trump waiving sanctions on Russia and striking a deal with Moscow on diesel.
Ukraine and its European allies have worried the White House is siding with Moscow, which launched Europe’s worst war since WWII in 2022.
Saint Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Flights were restricted at the city’s Pulkovo airport, Beglov said, adding that 12 housing blocks were also damaged.
Russia’s VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit in the city and Ozon -- Russia’s second largest retailer -- also reported a hit on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the 2022 war.
Ukraine has attacked Moscow and Saint Petersburg throughout the Kremlin’s dragging offensive but large-scale hits on Russia’s main cities are rare.
“The Kyiv regime is putting up a fight, but that cannot change the course of events,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media.
Russia’s offensive against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions. Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
US-led peace talks have not led to a breakthrough. In a fifth year of war, few see a way out. Putin appeared in military uniform this week and repeated Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
“There’s a general feeling: they’re attacking, we’re attacking -- it’s become the dreadful routine of war,” 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Sergei, another resident of the city who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
“I don’t know if I was scared, what must be will be,” he told AFP.
“My main thought was that petrol would run out at the petrol stations and I’d better fill up.”
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.
Leningrad governor Drozdenko said 20,000 people were without power in the town of Yanino, where a substation was hit.
He said a woman and three children were hospitalised “with symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning” in the region after drone debris fell on a house, causing a fire.
“I woke up at night, heard bangs, looked out of the window and there was a fire,” 40-year-old Saint Petersburg resident Igor told AFP.
“They’re getting on my nerves already,” he added, referring to Ukraine.
In Ukraine, Zelensky said Russian strikes hit substations in four Ukrainian regions, leaving “tens of thousands of families without power.”
Ukrainian authorities said Russian attacks killed at least three people Sunday, including a 27-year-old woman in Zaporizhzhia and two people in the western Volyn region bordering Poland.
The Saint Petersburg attack came a day after Zelensky called on allies to keep up pressure on Moscow as he denounced Trump’s move to block new sanctions on Russia.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” Zelensky said Sunday, adding:
“On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”
Trump this week blocked a package of new sanctions on Russia which was meant to target Putin, as well as Russia’s energy and defence sectors.
He also signed an agreement with Moscow this month to buy diesel, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of elections.
“It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance,” Zelensky said Sunday.

item.title: Muhammad bin Salman’s Humbling and the Return of the Ottomans
item.description:
The Houthis bloodied Saudi Crown Prince Muhammad bin Salman’s nose—again—with their deadly, cruel, but effective attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport last week. The strikes are the latest in a series of mostly self-inflicted setbacks—exacerbated by President Trump’s ill-considered war with Iran—that have frustrated the Crown Prince’s now decade-old aspirations to turn Saudi Arabia into a global economic, financial, and military powerhouse. Instead, MbS’s faltering economic reforms, combined with his bad bet on relying on Donald Trump as a security partner, are yet another reminder that Saudi Arabia is a weak state, dependent on and vulnerable to the whims of more powerful outside actors. And more than ever, the Saudis don’t have a good way out of that predicament.

The roots of MbS’s cascading problems lie in the early years of his de facto reign, which began in 2015, when he assumed the roles of defense minister and deputy crown prince. They stem from his personal arrogance and foreign misadventures, as well as his more admirable recognition—poorly acted upon—that the Saudi kingdom was, and remains, a relic in need of modernization and a future beyond hydrocarbons.

Over several years, MbS shattered Al Saud governing norms; alienated and pushed aside many members of the large and mostly indolent royal family; and sidelined the kingdom’s religious establishment (good riddance, say I). He also alienated neighbors such as Qatar and the UAE, ultimately to Saudi Arabia’s detriment, and started a war with the Houthis that he lost—and is now losing again.

MbS also unleashed much-needed economic and social reforms (women can now—gasp!—drive). The economy has gone from being mostly driven by government spending to being slightly less so. Homeownership is up, and unemployment among Saudis is down, according to IMF data. Nonreligious tourism grew from 2019 until last year, albeit from a low base. And Aramco’s kind-of, sort-of IPO in 2019 raised billions to support MbS’s ambitions in what was then the largest such offering in global equity history, although it now seems quaint beside the $85 billion SpaceX IPO.

But extravagant government spending in pursuit of unproductive, unachievable vanity projects (NEOM, anyone?) and MbS’s wild overestimation of the resources at his disposal are hobbling his ability to pursue the Vision 2030 economic reform program. And it turns out that, beyond the usual cadre of foreign finance bros and management consultants who are happy to bill the Saudi government by the hour or by the project, outside investors who could provide the capital and expertise needed to make the reforms viable are not convinced that Saudi Arabia is a place where they want to do business at the scale MbS needs. Net foreign direct investment in the kingdom last year was only about one-third of what the Saudi government had envisioned under Vision 2030. And, it goes without saying, 2026 is not proving to be a good year, with the IMF estimating that FDI will fall by about one-third.

The Crown Prince’s problems are not all of his own making, of course. But even so, his miscalculations have exacerbated the difficulties he is now struggling to address. The Iran war has scrambled the kingdom’s security and economic calculations, inviting Iran and its Houthi allies to prey on a country woefully unprepared for conflict despite decades of profligate but mostly ineffectual defense spending. The extravagant welcome MbS accorded Trump in Riyadh early last year has gained the Saudis mostly nothing. It’s not just that the Saudis—and other Gulf potentates, to be sure—assess that President Trump has treated them shabbily. It is that the American military has so far proved unable to achieve anything better than a stalemate against a third-rate regional power—Iran—with all the implications that sad fact holds for the region and for our global standing and credibility.

So where does this leave the now-middle-aged Crown Prince and the country he rules as he contemplates the coming decades of his reign? Recalibrating and scrambling, to be sure. Many of the investment megaprojects that were once cornerstones of his Vision 2030 program are dead or on life support. Three prominent examples are the now-bankrupt, Saudi-financed LIV Golf league; The Line at NEOM; and the absurdly overpriced, vanity-driven $50 billion giant cube, the Mukaab in Riyadh. And the economic pain is bleeding into other prestige projects as well, including the postponed (read: canceled) Asian Winter Games originally scheduled for 2029. The tens of billions spent—and the tens of billions more not spent because the country can’t afford it—have left the Saudis mostly where they were after all their past failed efforts to diversify the economy: reliant on hydrocarbons to sustain it and pay the government’s bills. Vision 2030 has changed that at the margins (and the vibes of living in and visiting the country are certainly different), but not in a fundamental way.

Compounding MbS’s woes, of course, is the regional security earthquake brought about by Trump’s Iran war. The United States is receding and retreating from its role as regional hegemon and the Crown Prince can be under no illusion that this will change after Trump leaves office in 2029. The Saudi brand is toxic among Democrats, and the emergence of the US as the global energy superpower under President Obama and during the first Trump administration has fundamentally changed the relationship between Riyadh and Washington. So, again, Riyadh is reduced to trying to do what it has always been forced to do: seek outside protection while also accommodating its adversaries.

The Crown Prince’s options are not good. His much-vaunted security agreement with Turkey and Pakistan demonstrates how poor his alternatives are to the now-defunct Pax Americana—and must also be personally humiliating. After all, one of his putative new protectors, President Erdoğan, gleefully embarrassed the then-young Crown Prince after Saudi agents murdered Jamal Khashoggi in Turkey in 2018. And anyone who has spent time in the kingdom knows well the lingering distaste for—and insecurity about—the country’s former Ottoman masters. As for Pakistan, it takes little imagination to understand how that benighted and impoverished country is viewed by the kingdom’s ruling family.

At a more practical level, Turkey and Pakistan will never replace the military capabilities of the United States, and both countries’ commitment to their new security agreement will be limited by the simple fact that Iran holds them at risk as well. Riyadh’s security strategy will probably closely resemble its current response to the Houthi threat, as detailed in a recent Wall Street Journal article: scouring the globe for weapons to defend against missiles and drones, contemplating hiring mercenaries to fight in Yemen in lieu of Saudi forces that are demonstrably not up to the task, and quietly seeking an accommodation with the Houthis to try to make the whole thing go away. In a region fundamentally altered by the US-Iran war—with US credibility as a security partner in tatters and Iran emboldened, if weakened—good luck with that.

item.title: The Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain away | Editorial
item.description:
Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong

Does Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history of chummy phone calls, high-profile meetings and attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees to negotiate Ukraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations.

Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales are falling from European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be a betrayal. European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened.

item.title: Saudi Arabia executes man over crimes allegedly committed as a child
item.description:
Saudi Arabia executes man over crimes allegedly committed as a child

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 10/20/2026 - 10:13
Human Rights Watch says Hassan al-Faraj was convicted over offences allegedly committed at 14, while Yousef al-Manasif faces execution after a Supreme Court ruling
Saudi Shia women during a protest against the execution of cleric Nimr al-Nimr in Qatif, Saudi Arabia, 8 January 2016 (STR/AFP)
Off

Saudi Arabia has executed a man convicted of offences allegedly committed when he was a child, according to Human Rights Watch (HRW).

Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, who was executed on Saturday, was convicted of offences allegedly committed when he was 14 years old, including "meeting and developing friendships with other detained and wanted individuals". 

“The execution of Hassan al-Faraj is unconscionable compounded by alleged torture-tainted evidence and a well-documented record of unfair trials,” said Joey Shea, HRW’s senior Saudi Arabia researcher.

“With the Supreme Court’s recent decision, Yousef al-Manasif is also at serious risk of execution,” she added.

Faraj was arrested in 2017 and sentenced to death by Saudi Arabia’s Specialised Criminal Court in 2022, according to HRW. 

His lawyers have said that he had been tortured and forced to sign a confession used in the case. HRW also reported that he was held in solitary confinement. 

Yousef al-Manasif, who was convicted over alleged offences committed when he was 15 and 16, is also at risk of execution after the Supreme Court reportedly upheld his sentence, according to the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR). 

Manasif was arrested in April 2017. He was accused of participating in protests against the Saudi authorities’ treatment of the country’s Shia minority and attending funeral processions in 2011 and 2012, when he was 15 and 16.

Bangladesh seeks answers after Saudi Arabia executes two of its citizens without notice
Read More »

A 2024 opinion adopted by the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found that the detention of Faraj, Manasif and three other men -  Jawad Qureiris, Abdullah al-Derazi and Jalal al-Labbad - was arbitrary and that their proceedings involved serious fair-trial violations.

It said their detention violated several provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and called for their immediate release and compensation. 

Saudi Arabia’s government disputed the allegations, saying the claims were unfounded and that the country’s laws and procedures complied with international human rights standards.

The UN working group’s report said Manasif alleged that he had been physically and psychologically tortured in detention and coerced into signing confessions later used against him. 

Another defendant, Ali al-Mabyook, was sentenced to death over alleged offences that included attending funeral processions before he turned 18, according to HRW and court documents. 

Coerced confessions

His case has also drawn concern from rights groups over the use of counterterrorism legislation and allegations of coerced confessions. 

Qureiris was sentenced to death in 2022 over alleged offences that included acts committed as a minor, according to the UN working group.

The group’s opinion said he had alleged that he was tortured and held in solitary confinement for 270 days to force a confession.

Saudi authorities executed Ali al-Subaiti on 9 April 2026, according to the Saudi Press Agency.

HRW said he had been sentenced to death over alleged offences that included participating in a demonstration when he was 12. 

Saudi Arabia’s 2018 Juvenile Law and a 2020 executive order introduced protections against imposing the death penalty for certain offences committed by people under 18. 

HRW has argued that the protections do not adequately cover defendants prosecuted under the kingdom’s counterterrorism legislation, leaving some people convicted over alleged childhood offences at risk of execution. 

“Saudi Arabia’s execution spree, particularly for offences by children, shows no signs of slowing down in 2026,” Shea said.

“This underscores the urgent need for the international community to press the Saudi government to immediately halt executions and abolish the death penalty once and for all.”

The initial term of the agreement is five years, said the release, adding, it will automatically be extended for another five years upon expiry. As a result, the overall term of the agreement will be 10 years.

Under the agreement, protection of Bangladeshi workers will be ensured, cooperation between the two countries in sending and receiving workers will be strengthened and opportunities for skills development through employment will be created.

Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury said, through this agreement, in addition to ensuring maximum protection for Bangladeshi workers, opportunities will be created for their skills development, higher wages and long-term residence in Japan.

He said that under the agreement, Bangladeshi workers will receive legal protection equivalent to that of local Japanese workers and equal opportunities for men and women in the workplace will be ensured.

Particularly female foreign workers cannot be dismissed or subjected to discriminatory treatment because of pregnancy or childbirth. For this reason, the agreement also does not contain any mandatory provision for forced repatriation, the release said.

It further said that during Prime Minister Tareque Rahman’s upcoming visit to Japan, copies of the agreement will be officially handed over between the two parties.

The ministry expressed hope that through the implementation of the agreement, the friendly relations between Bangladesh and Japan will be further strengthened, and opportunities for the development of Bangladesh’s skilled human resources will be expanded.

item.title: Rooppur plant eyes power start-up in October
item.description:
The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant (RNPP) is set to begin the power start-up phase likely this October, a key step towards generating electricity from the country’s first nuclear power facility.
Once the reactor’s output reaches 35% of capacity, supply to the national grid will begin. Officials say that, if everything goes according to plan, around 300 megawatts (MW) could be added to the grid in December.
A responsible source at the Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Limited (NPCBL) told Dhaka Tribune that the start-up would begin at zero to 1% power likely on October 25. Once output reaches 35%, 300MW can be supplied to the grid, which is the standard procedure.
“But numerous tests must be carried out to clear each stage,” the source said. After every increase in power, all parameters must be checked to ensure they are within limits.
According to the sources, it usually takes about 40 days to reach 35% power after the start-up begins. The timeline could stretch if any test fails along the way.
If all goes well, the plant could be ready for production in the last week of November, or else in December, they said.
Currently, tests on B-2 (fission reaction) are underway. After these are completed, and subject to approval from the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA), Stage-C, which is the power start-up, will begin shortly.
Stage-D, or trial operation, will follow next. During this phase, the plant will be tested through trials to establish that it can operate at full capacity. Power generation will be raised and lowered to test the grid’s capacity to absorb it. The plant will also be shut down briefly at times for testing.
Stage-D is expected to take around 10 months. During this period, Rooppur’s operators will work alongside the Russian contractor to build up their skills.
The sources said the plant is currently in the physics start-up stage, with every piece of equipment being tested at very low thermal power. Thermal power will then be raised to spin the turbine, and electricity generation will begin gradually.
Power will be increased step by step once everything checks out in the physics tests and BAERA gives its approval. BAERA’s permission will also be required for spinning the turbine and for generating electricity. At that point, officials will check whether the turbine and the generation process are functioning properly.
An official responsible for the construction project told local media: “If we follow the ideal programme, we hope the plant can go into production by December. But if we get stuck on any test at the last moment, it could take longer.”
Some people involved in the project, however, expressed doubt about meeting the December schedule. They said it is very difficult to give a fixed date for a nuclear plant to start production, and that even a minor problem could mean restarting work from scratch. Even so, December will remain the target.
A delegation from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is organising a training workshop to help ensure emergency preparedness and safety at Rooppur, sources said.
The IAEA’s Emergency Preparedness Review (EPREV) mission will run in Bangladesh from November 8 to 18, reviewing the country’s preparedness for nuclear emergencies.
Talking to Dhaka Tribune, Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, said bringing Rooppur’s emergency preparedness up to international standards would require coordination among the agencies concerned, trained manpower, clear written guidelines, and round-the-clock radiation and environmental monitoring.
BAERA Chairman Mahmudul Hasan said an integrated emergency response framework should be put in place before the IAEA delegation’s visit, with clearly defined responsibilities for everyone, from first responders in the field to national-level decision-makers.
Abul Khayer Md Akkas Ali, additional secretary of the Atomic Energy Division at the Science and Technology Ministry, said the government is committed to providing the necessary institutional support to ensure nuclear safety.
Meanwhile, earlier, Posts, Telecommunications, ICT Minister and Science and Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam said efforts are under way to supply around 300MW from Rooppur’s first reactor to the national grid by November.
He said the 1,200MW mega project is a flagship project for Russia’s Rosatom, which is therefore giving it high priority. Experts sent three months ago are working round the clock, he added.
The minister also said there is a plan to load fuel into the second reactor around June next year.
